sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: After 40 minutes of dark adaptation, the visual threshold is lowest at which wavelength?
w: Full dark adaptation is scotopic (rod-driven); rods peak at ~507 nm. 555 nm is the photopic cone peak.
decode: Fully dark-adapted vision is SCOTOPIC (rod-driven), and rods peak near 507 nm.
ow: 440 nm is the S-cone (blue) peak, a photopic value.
Correct. Dark-adapted vision is rod-driven; rods peak near 507 nm.
535 nm is the M-cone (green) peak, a cone value.
555 nm is the photopic cone peak, used in bright light, not after dark adaptation.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: How long does full, rod-based dark adaptation take?
w: Cones plateau at ~7 min (Kohlrausch kink); rhodopsin regenerates slowly, so full rod adaptation takes 30–40 min.
decode: Cones plateau at ~7 min, but rhodopsin regenerates slowly, so full ROD adaptation takes 30–40 min.
ow: Correct. Slow rhodopsin regeneration makes full rod adaptation take 30–40 minutes.
7 minutes is only the cone plateau (Kohlrausch kink), not full adaptation.
15 minutes is partway along the rod branch, not complete.
60 minutes overstates it; adaptation is essentially done by 40.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: The inflection point at ~7 minutes on the dark adaptation curve, where rods take over from cones, is the:
w: The Kohlrausch kink marks the cone-to-rod transition at about 7 minutes.
decode: The KOHLRAUSCH KINK is the ~7-minute break where cones plateau and rods take over.
ow: Ricco's law is spatial summation, not a point on the adaptation curve.
The Stiles-Crawford effect is directional sensitivity of cones, not a curve inflection.
The Purkinje shift is the 555→507 nm sensitivity change, not the 7-minute break.
Correct. The Kohlrausch kink is the ~7-minute cone-to-rod handover.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: On Hirschberg the corneal reflex sits temporal in both eyes, but cover test shows no movement. The cause is:
w: Positive kappa puts the pupil nasal to the visual axis, so the reflex looks temporal, mimicking exotropia. Negative cover test confirms pseudo-exo.
decode: POSITIVE kappa puts the pupil NASAL, so the reflex looks temporal, giving pseudo-exotropia, confirmed by a negative cover test.
ow: Correct. Positive kappa shifts the pupil nasal, making the reflex look temporal with no real deviation.
Angle alpha is measured at the nodal point and does not itself produce this reflex-plus-negative-cover picture.
True exotropia would show outward movement on cover test; here there is none.
Esotropia gives a nasal-looking reflex and inward cover movement, the opposite.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: A nasally displaced corneal light reflex with a negative cover test indicates:
w: Negative kappa puts the pupil temporal, so the reflex sits nasal, simulating esotropia (pseudo-eso).
decode: NEGATIVE kappa puts the pupil TEMPORAL, so the reflex sits nasal, giving pseudo-esotropia, confirmed by a negative cover test.
ow: True esotropia would show inward movement on cover test; here there is none.
True exotropia gives a temporal-looking reflex, the opposite pattern.
Correct. Negative kappa shifts the pupil temporal, making the reflex look nasal with no real deviation.
Positive kappa shifts the pupil nasal and mimics exotropia, not esotropia.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Rhodopsin fails to regenerate after light exposure. Which step is impaired?
o: Re-isomerization of retinal in the RPE
Cone pigment synthesis in the fovea
Glutamate release in the dark current
w: The visual cycle regenerates 11-cis retinal from all-trans retinal in the RPE; blocking it stops rhodopsin regeneration.
decode: Rhodopsin regeneration needs 11-cis retinal remade from all-trans retinal in the RPE; block that and regeneration stops.
ow: Correct. Re-isomerization of retinal happens in the RPE and is the regeneration step.
Photoisomerization is the light-triggered step, not the regeneration that follows.
Cone pigment synthesis is separate from rod rhodopsin regeneration.
Glutamate release is dark-current synaptic activity, unrelated to regeneration.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Which is true of the fovea?
o: Equal numbers of rods and cones
w: The fovea excludes rods entirely and holds the highest cone density (~150,000/mm²) for peak acuity.
decode: The fovea excludes rods entirely and holds the highest CONE density for peak acuity.
ow: The fovea is packed with cones, not devoid of photoreceptors; that describes the optic disc.
Rods and cones are not equal here; the fovea is essentially all cones.
Rod density peaks in the periphery, not the fovea.
Correct. The fovea has no rods and the densest cones.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Why is a dim star easier to see by looking slightly to the side of it?
o: Rods peak at ~20° from the fovea
w: Averted vision lands the image on peripheral retina where rod density peaks (~20°), maximizing scotopic sensitivity.
k: Averted vision targets peak rod zone (~20°).
decode: Averted vision lands the image on peripheral retina where ROD density peaks (~20°), maximizing dim-light sensitivity.
ow: Accommodation focuses the image; it does not boost peripheral sensitivity for a dim star.
Cones are densest at the fovea, not off-center.
The blind spot is not central; it is ~15° temporal.
Correct. Rods peak ~20° from the fovea, so looking to the side aids scotopic detection.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: In the axes of Fick, the anteroposterior (Y) axis, 24 mm long, controls which movement?
w: The AP axis is longest (24 mm) and controls torsion. X = vertical, Z = horizontal.
decode: The anteroposterior (Y) axis is the longest (24 mm) and rotation about it produces TORSION.
ow: Correct. The AP/Y axis controls torsion.
Vertical movements are about the X (transverse) axis.
Horizontal movements are about the Z (vertical) axis.
Vergence is a binocular act, not a single Fick axis.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: The vertical (Z) axis controls which eye movement?
w: Rotation about the vertical axis produces horizontal movements. The X (transverse) axis produces vertical movements.
decode: Rotation about the vertical (Z) axis produces HORIZONTAL movements.
ow: Vertical movements are produced about the X (transverse) axis.
Correct. The vertical Z axis produces horizontal movement.
Torsion is produced about the anteroposterior Y axis.
The eye does move about the Z axis, so 'no movement' is wrong.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Angle alpha is measured at which point?
w: Angle alpha (optical vs visual axis) is measured at the nodal point; angle kappa is measured at the pupil.
k: Alpha at nodal point; kappa at pupil.
decode: Angle ALPHA (optical vs visual axis) is measured at the NODAL point; kappa is measured at the pupil.
ow: The fovea is where the visual axis lands, not where alpha is measured.
The pupil center is the reference for angle kappa, not alpha.
Correct. Angle alpha is measured at the nodal point.
The center of rotation is where the Fick axes cross, not the alpha reference.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: At dusk a blue flower looks brighter than a red one that seemed equal at noon. This is the:
w: As light fades, sensitivity shifts from the photopic 555 nm peak to the scotopic 507 nm (blue-green) peak, so blues relatively brighten.
decode: As light fades, peak sensitivity shifts from 555 nm to the scotopic 507 nm, so blues relatively brighten: the PURKINJE shift.
ow: Correct. The Purkinje shift moves peak sensitivity toward blue-green in dim light.
The Stiles-Crawford effect is directional cone sensitivity, not a dusk brightness change.
The Bezold-Brucke shift is a hue change with intensity, not this scotopic brightening.
Troxler fading is disappearance of a steady peripheral image, unrelated.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Ricco's law describes which kind of summation?
w: Ricco's law: within the critical area, area × intensity is constant (spatial). Bunsen-Roscoe covers temporal summation.
decode: Ricco's law is SPATIAL summation: within the critical area, area × intensity is constant.
ow: Temporal summation is governed by Bunsen-Roscoe, not Ricco.
There is no 'chromatic summation' law by this name.
Binocular summation is a separate two-eye effect.
Correct. Ricco's law describes spatial summation.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: The law stating that time × intensity is constant for a brief stimulus (temporal summation) is:
w: Bunsen-Roscoe governs temporal summation (up to ~100 ms for rods).
decode: Bunsen-Roscoe governs TEMPORAL summation: time × intensity is constant for a brief stimulus.
ow: Weber's law is about the just-noticeable difference ratio, not temporal summation.
Bloch's law is another name here but is offered as an 'exception', which is wrong.
Correct. Bunsen-Roscoe covers temporal summation.
Ricco's law is spatial (area × intensity), not temporal.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Which cone pigment is most sensitive to long-wavelength (red) light?
w: Erythrolabe (L-cones, ~750 nm) = red; chlorolabe (M, 535 nm) = green; cyanolabe (S, 440 nm) = blue.
decode: ERYTHROLABE is the long-wavelength (red) L-cone pigment.
ow: Rhodopsin is the rod pigment, not a red cone pigment.
Chlorolabe is the green (M-cone) pigment.
Cyanolabe is the blue (S-cone) pigment.
Correct. Erythrolabe is the red L-cone pigment.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: All three axes of eye rotation pass through the center of rotation, located approximately:
w: The center of rotation is ~13.5 mm behind the cornea; all axes of Fick pass through it.
k: Center of rotation 13.5 mm behind cornea.
decode: The center of rotation, where all Fick axes cross, sits ~13.5 mm behind the cornea.
ow: 24 mm is the axial length of the globe, not the center of rotation.
The nodal point is an optical reference, not the mechanical center of rotation.
6.5 mm is far too shallow for the center of rotation.
Correct. The center of rotation is ~13.5 mm behind the cornea.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Compared with the cone plateau, rods at full dark adaptation are about:
w: Dark adaptation improves threshold by ~3 log units, making rods roughly 1000× more sensitive than cones.
decode: Dark adaptation improves threshold by ~3 log units, making rods roughly 1000× more sensitive than cones.
ow: 10× understates it by two log units.
100× is one log unit short of the ~3 log improvement.
Rods end up far more sensitive than cones, not equal.
Correct. ~3 log units means about 1000× greater rod sensitivity.

sec: B1 Visual System and Ocular Optics
q: Which lowers the visual threshold (increases sensitivity)?
w: Binocular viewing combines neural signals from both eyes, lowering threshold. A larger pupil also helps.
k: Two eyes beat one for threshold.
decode: Binocular viewing combines both eyes' neural signals, LOWERING threshold (higher sensitivity).
ow: Correct. Two eyes summate neurally, lowering threshold.
A smaller pupil lets in less light, raising threshold.
Monocular viewing loses binocular summation, so it is less sensitive.
A bright background raises threshold, the opposite of what is asked.

q: In early optic neuritis, which visual function is affected earliest?
w: Color is the most vulnerable function (basis of the red-desaturation test); motion is the most resilient.
decode: COLOR is the most vulnerable function in optic nerve disease; it fails first (basis of red desaturation).
ow: Low-frequency contrast is not the earliest loss; color goes first.
Correct. Color conduction is the most vulnerable and drops out earliest.
Motion is the most resilient function, lost last.
Form is more resilient than color.

q: Which visual function is the most resilient, lost last in optic nerve disease?
w: Motion perception survives longest; color is lost first.
decode: MOTION perception is the most resilient function, lost last in optic nerve disease.
ow: Stereopsis is not the most resilient single function tested here.
Fine acuity degrades before motion.
Correct. Motion is the most resilient, lost last.
Color is the most vulnerable, lost first.

q: Which LGB (lateral geniculate body) layers receive contralateral (crossed) input?
w: Layers 1, 4, 6 are contralateral (nasal/crossed); layers 2, 3, 5 are ipsilateral (temporal/uncrossed).
decode: LGB layers 1, 4, 6 receive CONTRALATERAL (crossed, nasal) input.
ow: Layer 1 alone is incomplete; crossed input is in 1, 4 and 6.
Not all six; the eyes alternate across layers.
Correct. Layers 1, 4, 6 are contralateral.
Layers 2, 3, 5 are ipsilateral, not contralateral.

q: The primary visual cortex (area 17) is mainly responsible for:
w: Area 17 detects basic features. Object recognition needs the ventral stream through areas 18, 19, and inferotemporal cortex.
k: Area 17 = basic features, not object ID.
decode: Area 17 (primary visual cortex) detects BASIC FEATURES, not whole-object identity.
ow: Color naming is a higher-order function beyond area 17.
Correct. Area 17 performs basic feature detection.
Object recognition needs the ventral stream beyond area 17.
Eye-movement planning is a frontal/brainstem role, not area 17.

q: The ventral visual stream is responsible for:
w: Ventral ('what') runs to the temporal lobe; dorsal ('where/how') runs to the parietal lobe.
decode: The VENTRAL ('what') stream runs to the temporal lobe for object recognition.
ow: Correct. The ventral stream handles 'what' object recognition.
Accommodation is a reflex, not a ventral-stream perceptual task.
'Where/how' spatial and motion processing is the dorsal stream.
Pupil reflexes are subcortical, not ventral-stream.

q: The dorsal visual stream processes:
w: The dorsal stream handles 'where/how' (spatial and motion) and projects to the parietal lobe.
decode: The DORSAL ('where/how') stream runs to the parietal lobe for spatial location and motion.
ow: Object identity is the ventral 'what' stream.
Face recognition is a ventral-stream function.
Correct. The dorsal stream processes spatial location and motion.
Color is processed in the ventral pathway, not the dorsal.

q: Background intensity doubles from 100 to 200 units. By Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference (JND):
w: Weber's law: ΔI/I = k. The ratio is constant, so when I doubles, the absolute JND doubles.
decode: Weber's law keeps ΔI/I constant, so when I doubles the absolute JND DOUBLES.
ow: The JND does not stay a fixed absolute value; the ratio is what stays fixed.
Correct. Constant ratio means the JND doubles when the background doubles.
It does not halve; a bigger background needs a bigger difference.
The JND does not disappear at high intensity.

q: The red-desaturation test (a red target looks washed out in one eye) detects:
w: Because color conduction is the most vulnerable, red desaturation flags early optic nerve compromise.
k: Red desaturation = early optic nerve disease.
decode: Because color conduction is most vulnerable, red desaturation flags EARLY optic nerve disease.
ow: Correct. Red desaturation signals early optic nerve compromise.
Cataract dims and yellows overall, not selective red desaturation between eyes.
Refractive error blurs; it does not desaturate red.
A macular hole gives central metamorphopsia, not monocular red washout.

q: Area 18 of the visual cortex is best described as:
w: Area 17 = primary striate; area 18 = parastriate (secondary); area 19 = peristriate (higher).
decode: Area 18 is the PARASTRIATE cortex (secondary visual area).
ow: The lateral geniculate is a thalamic relay, not area 18.
Primary striate cortex is area 17, not 18.
Peristriate cortex is area 19.
Correct. Area 18 is the parastriate cortex.

q: A lesion isolated to area 17 of one hemisphere would most directly impair:
w: Area 17 is primary visual cortex; damage causes a contralateral field defect of basic vision.
decode: Area 17 is primary visual cortex; a one-sided lesion drops the CONTRALATERAL field.
ow: Object naming needs higher areas and both fields would not be equally hit by one-sided area 17 damage.
Correct. A unilateral area 17 lesion causes a contralateral field defect.
Motion loss alone points to area V5, not area 17.
Color loss alone points to V4, not area 17.

q: Object recognition (the 'what' pathway) requires processing beyond area 17 through:
o: The dorsal stream to parietal lobe
The ventral stream to IT cortex
w: Recognition is a ventral-stream function extending to inferotemporal cortex; area 17 alone only detects features.
k: Recognition = ventral stream to IT cortex.
decode: Object recognition extends beyond area 17 through the VENTRAL stream to inferotemporal cortex.
ow: The dorsal stream to parietal handles 'where/how', not object recognition.
The pretectal nuclei serve pupil reflexes, not recognition.
The superior colliculus tectum handles orienting, not object identity.
Correct. Recognition runs via the ventral stream to IT cortex.

q: Which LGB layers carry ipsilateral (uncrossed, temporal retina) input?
w: Layers 2, 3, 5 are ipsilateral; 1, 4, 6 are contralateral.
decode: LGB layers 2, 3, 5 carry IPSILATERAL (uncrossed, temporal-retina) input.
ow: Not all layers; the eyes alternate.
Correct. Layers 2, 3, 5 are ipsilateral.
The eyes are segregated by layer, so 'none' is wrong.
Layers 1, 4, 6 are contralateral, not ipsilateral.

q: Weber's law is the physiological basis of which clinical measurement?
w: Because the JND scales with background intensity, contrast detection (ΔI/I) underlies contrast sensitivity testing.
decode: Because the JND scales with background, Weber's law underlies CONTRAST sensitivity testing.
ow: Correct. Weber's law is the basis of contrast sensitivity.
Color vision rests on cone opponency, not Weber's law.
Stereoacuity depends on retinal disparity, not Weber's law.
Visual acuity is a resolution limit, not a Weber-law contrast measure.

q: The normal temporal extent of the monocular visual field is:
w: Temporal is widest at 100°. Superior 60°, inferior 75°, nasal 60°.
decode: The TEMPORAL field is widest at 100° (nasal/superior 60°, inferior 75°).
ow: 60° is the nasal and superior extent, not temporal.
75° is the inferior extent.
Correct. Temporal extent is the widest at 100°.
120° is the binocular overlap, not a monocular temporal extent.

q: The normal nasal and superior extents of the visual field are about:
w: Nasal and superior are each ~60°; inferior 75°; temporal 100°.
decode: Nasal and superior extents are each ~60°.
ow: 45° understates the nasal/superior extent.
Correct. Nasal and superior are ~60° each.
75° is the inferior extent.
100° is the temporal extent.

q: The inferior extent of the normal visual field is approximately:
w: Inferior is ~75°, between nasal/superior (60°) and temporal (100°).
decode: The INFERIOR extent is ~75°, between the 60° nasal/superior and 100° temporal.
ow: 45° is too small for the inferior field.
60° is the nasal/superior extent.
Correct. Inferior extent is ~75°.
100° is the temporal extent.

q: How much of the visual field is seen binocularly?
w: The central 120° overlaps binocularly; each side has a 30° monocular temporal crescent.
decode: The central 120° overlaps binocularly; each side adds a 30° monocular crescent.
ow: 60° is a single monocular extent, not the binocular overlap.
90° understates the binocular field.
Correct. About 120° is seen binocularly.
180° is the full both-eyes horizontal span, not the binocular overlap.

q: The monocular temporal crescent (seen by one eye only) is about:
w: Beyond the 120° binocular zone, each eye sees a 30° temporal crescent alone.
decode: Beyond the 120° binocular zone, each eye alone sees a 30° temporal crescent.
ow: 90° overstates the crescent.
Correct. The monocular temporal crescent is ~30° each side.
10° understates it.
60° each side is too wide for the crescent.

q: On Goldmann perimetry, which stimulus size is the largest?
w: Size V (64 mm²) is largest, used to map peripheral field in RP and low vision; size I is smallest.
decode: Goldmann size V (64 mm²) is the LARGEST stimulus; size I is smallest.
ow: Size 0 is smaller than I, not the largest.
Correct. Size V is the largest Goldmann stimulus.
Size I is the smallest.
Size III is mid-range, not the largest.

q: The smallest Goldmann stimulus is:
w: Size I (0.25 mm²) is the smallest; size V (64 mm²) is the largest.
decode: Goldmann size I (0.25 mm²) is the SMALLEST stimulus; size V is largest.
ow: Size III is mid-range, not the smallest.
Correct. Size I is the smallest Goldmann stimulus.
Size V is the largest.
Size 0 is not the standard smallest used clinically here; I is the reference smallest.

q: The standard Goldmann perimeter background luminance is:
w: Goldmann uses a 31.5 apostilb background in a bowl of 300 mm radius.
decode: Goldmann uses a 31.5 apostilb background in a 300 mm bowl.
ow: Correct. The Goldmann background is 31.5 apostilbs.
10 apostilbs is not the Goldmann standard.
100 apostilbs is too bright for the standard.
3.15 apostilbs is off by a factor of ten.

q: The Amsler grid tests which portion of the visual field?
w: Each square is 1°; the grid covers only the central 10°, used for macular disease (metamorphopsia).
decode: The Amsler grid tests only the CENTRAL 10° for macular disease.
ow: The peripheral crescent is not what the Amsler grid samples.
The grid covers only the central 10°, not the full field.
The blind spot is not the Amsler target.
Correct. Each square is 1° and the grid covers the central 10°.

q: A bitemporal hemianopia localizes the lesion to the:
w: Crossing nasal fibers at the chiasm are damaged, producing bitemporal hemianopia, classically from a pituitary adenoma.
decode: BITEMPORAL hemianopia comes from damage to crossing nasal fibers at the CHIASM.
ow: An optic nerve lesion causes a monocular defect, not bitemporal.
An occipital lesion causes a congruous homonymous defect.
An optic tract lesion causes a homonymous hemianopia.
Correct. Bitemporal hemianopia localizes to the chiasm.

q: A superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky') localizes to:
w: Inferior retinal fibers loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop); damage gives a contralateral superior quadrant defect.
k: Pie in the sky = Meyer's loop (temporal).
decode: A 'pie in the sky' superior quadrantanopia localizes to MEYER'S LOOP in the temporal lobe.
ow: An optic nerve lesion gives a monocular defect, not a quadrant.
Correct. Inferior fibers loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop).
A chiasm lesion gives bitemporal hemianopia.
Parietal radiations give an inferior ('pie on the floor') defect.

q: Severely constricted fields with a small central island, plus years of night blindness, suggest:
w: RP is a rod dystrophy: a ring scotoma expands to leave a central island, with early nyctalopia.
decode: Constricted fields with a central island plus night blindness point to RETINITIS PIGMENTOSA.
ow: Correct. RP is a rod dystrophy: ring scotoma to central island with early nyctalopia.
Central serous retinopathy gives a central scotoma, not peripheral constriction.
A pituitary adenoma gives bitemporal hemianopia.
Glaucoma gives arcuate defects and nasal steps, not this pattern with night blindness.

q: Within the visual field, which function is the most vulnerable (lost first)?
w: Color is the most vulnerable; motion is the most resilient.
k: Color most vulnerable, motion most resilient.
decode: Within the visual field, COLOR is the most vulnerable function (lost first).
ow: Light detection is among the most resilient, not the first lost.
Form is more resilient than color.
Correct. Color is the most vulnerable, lost first.
Motion is the most resilient, lost last.

q: The most common color vision deficiency is:
w: Deuteranomaly (weak green) is most common; tritan defects are rare and autosomal.
decode: DEUTERANOMALY (weak green) is the most common color deficiency.
ow: Tritan defects are rare, not the most common.
Protanopia is less common than deuteranomaly.
Achromatopsia is very rare.
Correct. Deuteranomaly is the most common defect.

q: Additive mixing of red, green, and blue light produces:
w: Additive (light) mixing R+G+B = white; subtractive (pigment) mixing C+M+Y = black.
decode: ADDITIVE mixing of R+G+B light produces WHITE.
ow: Black results from subtractive mixing, not additive light.
Yellow is R+G only, not all three.
Correct. Additive R+G+B light gives white.
Gray is not the result of full additive mixing.

q: Subtractive mixing of cyan, magenta, and yellow pigments produces:
w: Subtractive pigment mixing C+M+Y = black; additive light mixing gives white.
decode: SUBTRACTIVE mixing of C+M+Y pigments produces BLACK.
ow: Green is a two-pigment mix, not all three.
Red is not the full-pigment result.
Correct. Subtractive C+M+Y pigment gives black.
White comes from additive light mixing, not pigments.

q: What is the purpose of Ishihara plate 1 (the '12' plate)?
w: Plate 1 is the control: everyone, including color-deficient patients, reads it. It confirms task understanding.
decode: Ishihara plate 1 is a CONTROL plate everyone reads, confirming task understanding.
ow: It is not a plate only normals see.
It does not detect tritan defects.
Correct. Plate 1 is the control that all patients can read.
It is not a protan-only plate.

q: To precisely classify the axis and severity of a color defect, the best test is:
w: The Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test plots a total error score and the exact axis of confusion. Ishihara only screens red-green.
decode: The FM-100 Hue test plots a total error score and the exact axis and severity of a color defect.
ow: Plate 1 is only a control plate, not a classifier.
FALANT is an occupational pass/fail lantern test.
Correct. The FM-100 Hue test classifies axis and severity.
Ishihara only screens red-green, without grading severity.

q: The trichromatic theory of color (at the receptor level) is credited to:
w: Young-Helmholtz = trichromatic (three cones, receptor level); Hering = opponent process (post-receptor).
decode: YOUNG-HELMHOLTZ trichromatic theory operates at the receptor level (three cones).
ow: Ladd-Franklin proposed an evolutionary color theory, not the classic trichromatic one.
Correct. Young-Helmholtz is the trichromatic (three-cone) theory.
Hering proposed the opponent-process (post-receptor) theory.
Purkinje is known for the dim-light sensitivity shift, not a color theory.

q: The opponent-process theory of color (post-receptor level) is credited to:
w: Hering proposed opponent channels (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white) at the post-receptor level.
decode: HERING proposed opponent channels (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white) at the post-receptor level.
ow: Correct. Hering's opponent-process theory is post-receptor.
Young-Helmholtz is the receptor-level trichromatic theory.
Ladd-Franklin proposed an evolutionary theory, not opponent process.
Newton described the spectrum, not the opponent-process theory.

q: The S-cone pigment cyanolabe is most sensitive at about:
w: Cyanolabe (S-cone) peaks ~440 nm (blue); chlorolabe ~535 nm (green); erythrolabe ~750 nm (red).
decode: Cyanolabe (S-cone) peaks near 440 nm (blue).
ow: Correct. Cyanolabe peaks ~440 nm.
507 nm is the rod (rhodopsin) peak.
535 nm is the M-cone (green) peak.
750 nm is the L-cone (red) region.

q: In protanopia, red light appears:
w: Without L-cones, red light poorly stimulates the remaining cones, so reds look dim.
decode: Without L-cones, red light poorly stimulates remaining cones, so reds look DIM.
ow: Red does not appear brighter without L-cones.
Red is not seen unchanged in protanopia.
Protanopes confuse reds with dark tones, but the key change is loss of luminance, not turning green.
Correct. Missing L-cones make red appear dim.

q: How does the HRR test differ from Ishihara?
w: HRR (using symbols) screens both red-green and blue-yellow; Ishihara screens red-green only.
decode: HRR (symbol-based) screens BOTH red-green and blue-yellow; Ishihara screens red-green only.
ow: Correct. HRR tests both red-green and blue-yellow.
Screening red-green only describes Ishihara, not HRR.
HRR still needs a response; being response-free is not its distinction.
HRR uses symbols, not numeral plates.

q: The FALANT (Farnsworth Lantern) is primarily a(n):
w: FALANT is an occupational lantern test (e.g., for navigation/aviation), performed at 8 feet, not a diagnostic axis test.
decode: FALANT is an OCCUPATIONAL lantern pass/fail test, done at 8 feet.
ow: FALANT does not map the diagnostic axis of a defect.
It is not a stereo test.
Correct. FALANT is an occupational pass/fail lantern test.
It does not test the macula.

q: The prevalence of red-green color deficiency in males is approximately:
w: Red-green deficiency affects ~8% of males (X-linked), versus ~0.5% of females.
decode: Red-green deficiency affects ~8% of males (X-linked).
ow: 0.5% is roughly the female prevalence, not male.
2% understates the male prevalence.
Correct. About 8% of males have red-green deficiency.
20% overstates it.

q: Tritan (blue-yellow) congenital color defects are:
w: Congenital tritanopia is rare and autosomal, unlike the common X-linked red-green defects.
decode: Congenital TRITAN defects are RARE and AUTOSOMAL, unlike X-linked red-green.
ow: Tritan defects are autosomal, not X-linked like red-green.
Correct. Tritan defects are rare and autosomal.
Tritan is rare, not the most common defect.
Congenital tritan defects are inherited, not always acquired.

q: What is the normal AC/A ratio?
w: Normal AC/A is 4:1 to 6:1. High AC/A drives excess conditions; low AC/A drives insufficiency.
decode: Normal AC/A is 4:1 to 6:1.
ow: 12:1 to 15:1 is abnormally high.
1:1 to 2:1 is abnormally low.
Correct. Normal AC/A is 4:1 to 6:1.
8:1 to 10:1 is high.

q: A high AC/A ratio is associated with which conditions?
w: High AC/A = too much convergence per diopter = excess conditions (CE, DE).
decode: A HIGH AC/A means too much convergence per diopter, driving EXCESS conditions (CE, DE).
ow: Correct. High AC/A is linked to convergence excess and divergence excess.
Fusional vergence dysfunction has a normal AC/A.
Basic phorias have a roughly normal AC/A.
Insufficiency conditions go with a low AC/A, not high.

q: Convergence insufficiency is characterized by:
o: Low AC/A, exo at near, receded NPC
w: CI has a low AC/A, exophoria greater at near, and a receded NPC, with near symptoms.
k: CI = low AC/A, near exo, receded NPC.
decode: Convergence insufficiency has a LOW AC/A, exophoria greater at near, and a receded NPC.
ow: High AC/A with eso at near describes convergence excess, not CI.
Correct. CI shows low AC/A, near exophoria, and a receded NPC.
Normal AC/A with equal deviation does not fit CI.
Eso at distance is not the CI pattern.

q: Which is the slowest eye movement system?
w: Vergence is slowest (~20°/s). Saccades are fastest (500–1000°/s); VOR has the shortest latency.
decode: VERGENCE is the slowest eye-movement system (~20°/s).
ow: Saccades are the fastest movement, not the slowest.
Correct. Vergence is the slowest system.
Smooth pursuit is faster than vergence.
The VOR is a very fast reflex, not the slowest.

q: Which eye movement has the shortest (fastest) latency?
w: The VOR has ~15 ms latency, the fastest reflex, stabilizing gaze during head movement.
decode: The VESTIBULO-OCULAR REFLEX has the shortest latency (~15 ms).
ow: Smooth pursuit has a longer latency than the VOR.
Saccades have ~200 ms latency, slower to start than the VOR.
Vergence is the slowest system.
Correct. The VOR has the shortest latency.

q: Saccadic velocity is approximately:
w: Saccades are the fastest voluntary movement at 500–1000°/s; vergence is the slowest.
decode: Saccades are the fastest movement at 500–1000°/s.
ow: 20°/s is vergence velocity, not saccadic.
5°/s is far too slow for a saccade.
Correct. Saccadic velocity is 500–1000°/s.
90°/s understates saccadic speed.

q: Sheard's criterion for comfortable fusion requires the fusional reserve to be at least:
w: Sheard's: compensating fusional reserve ≥ 2× the phoria. An 8 PD exophoria needs ≥16 PD PFC.
decode: Sheard's criterion: the compensating fusional reserve should be at least TWICE the phoria.
ow: Three times the phoria overstates Sheard's requirement.
Correct. Sheard's requires reserve ≥ 2× the phoria.
Equal to the phoria is below Sheard's threshold.
Half the phoria is far below the requirement.

q: Percival's criterion states that the phoria should fall within:
o: The first third of the range
The middle third of the fusional range
w: Percival's: the demand line (phoria) should sit in the middle third of the total fusional vergence range.
decode: Percival's criterion: the demand (phoria) should sit in the MIDDLE THIRD of the fusional range.
ow: 'Twice the reserve' is not Percival's rule.
The blur point is a finding, not Percival's criterion.
The first third is where the demand should NOT sit.
Correct. Percival's places the demand in the middle third of the range.

q: In Worth's classification, simultaneous macular perception is:
w: Grade 1 = simultaneous perception, Grade 2 = flat fusion, Grade 3 = stereopsis.
decode: Worth Grade 1 is SIMULTANEOUS macular perception.
ow: Correct. Grade 1 is simultaneous perception.
Grade 3 is stereopsis.
Grade 2 is flat fusion.
It is graded; Grade 1 covers it.

q: In Worth's classification, flat (superimposition) fusion with amplitude is:
w: Grade 2 is fusion (merging two images, with vergence amplitude). Grade 3 is stereopsis.
decode: Worth Grade 2 is FLAT (superimposition) fusion with amplitude.
ow: There is no Grade 4 in Worth's three-grade scheme.
Correct. Grade 2 is flat fusion.
Grade 3 is stereopsis.
Grade 1 is simultaneous perception.

q: Hering's law of equal innervation applies to:
w: Hering's law governs binocular yoke muscles (equal innervation). Sherrington's is the monocular agonist-antagonist rule.
decode: Hering's law of equal innervation governs binocular YOKE muscles.
ow: Hering's law is not about the pupil.
Correct. Hering's law applies to yoke muscles of both eyes.
A single muscle is governed by neither of these binocular laws.
Agonist-antagonist within one eye is Sherrington's, not Hering's.

q: Sherrington's law of reciprocal innervation describes:
w: Sherrington's law is monocular: when the agonist contracts, its antagonist relaxes.
decode: Sherrington's law is monocular: agonist contracts while its antagonist RELAXES.
ow: The near accommodative response is not Sherrington's law.
Equal innervation to yoke muscles is Hering's law.
The pupillary reflex is not this reciprocal-innervation rule.
Correct. Sherrington's law: agonist contracts, antagonist relaxes.

q: An object beyond (farther than) the fixation point produces what physiologic diplopia?
w: Far objects stimulate nasal retina, giving uncrossed (homonymous) diplopia; near objects give crossed.
decode: An object BEYOND fixation stimulates nasal retina, giving UNCROSSED (homonymous) diplopia.
ow: Physiologic diplopia here is horizontal, not vertical.
There is diplopia, not none, for a non-fixated object.
Correct. Far objects give uncrossed diplopia.
Crossed diplopia is for near objects, not far.

q: An object closer than the fixation point produces:
w: Near objects stimulate temporal retina, producing crossed (heteronymous) diplopia.
decode: An object CLOSER than fixation stimulates temporal retina, giving CROSSED (heteronymous) diplopia.
ow: A near object is not suppressed in normal physiologic diplopia.
Correct. Near objects give crossed diplopia.
Uncrossed diplopia is for far objects, not near.
Physiologic diplopia here is horizontal, not torsional.

q: Normal retinal correspondence (NRC) is maintained in:
w: In heterophoria, binocular vision is kept most of the time, preserving NRC. Constant strabismus may develop ARC.
decode: Normal retinal correspondence is preserved in HETEROPHORIA, where fusion keeps the eyes aligned most of the time.
ow: Eccentric fixation is a monocular anomaly, not where NRC is maintained.
Constant strabismus may develop anomalous correspondence.
Deep amblyopia disrupts normal correspondence.
Correct. Heterophoria preserves NRC.

q: Anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC) typically develops in:
w: A fixed, constant deviation gives the brain time to rewire correspondence (ARC) to avoid diplopia.
decode: ARC develops in CONSTANT strabismus with a fixed angle, giving the brain time to rewire.
ow: Intermittent exophoria preserves normal correspondence.
Correct. A fixed constant deviation breeds ARC.
Uncorrected refractive error alone does not create ARC.
Long-standing orthophoria keeps normal correspondence.

q: In harmonious ARC, the anomalous neutral point:
o: Is less than the angle of deviation
w: Harmonious ARC is fully adapted: the anomalous angle equals the objective angle of deviation.
decode: In HARMONIOUS ARC, the anomalous angle EQUALS the objective angle of deviation.
ow: Less than the deviation describes unharmonious ARC.
Correct. Harmonious ARC: neutral point equals the deviation.
Exceeding the deviation is not the harmonious pattern.
The anomalous neutral point does exist in ARC.

q: The normal near point of convergence (NPC) break is:
w: Normal NPC break is ≤8 cm; greater than 10 cm suggests convergence insufficiency.
decode: Normal NPC break is ≤8 cm; beyond ~10 cm suggests convergence insufficiency.
ow: 25 cm indicates a markedly receded NPC.
20 cm is well beyond normal.
15 cm is receded, not normal.
Correct. Normal NPC break is ≤8 cm.

q: Panum's fusional area at the fovea is about:
w: Panum's area is very small at the fovea (6–10 arc min) and broadens peripherally.
decode: Panum's fusional area at the FOVEA is small (6–10 arc min) and widens peripherally.
ow: 30 arc min is wider than the foveal value.
Correct. Panum's area at the fovea is 6–10 arc min.
60 arc min is too wide for the fovea.
1 degree is far too wide for the foveal area.

q: A hyperope who is straight at distance but crosses at near, with a high AC/A, has:
w: Accommodative esotropia: hyperopic accommodation drives excess convergence (high AC/A), crossing the eyes at near.
decode: A hyperope straight at distance but crossing at near with high AC/A has ACCOMMODATIVE ESOTROPIA.
ow: Basic exophoria diverges, opposite to crossing at near.
Correct. Hyperopic accommodation drives excess convergence (high AC/A), crossing the eyes at near.
Divergence excess shows exo at distance, not eso at near.
Convergence insufficiency shows exo at near, not eso.

q: For an exophoria, vision therapy and prism approaches aim to:
w: Exophoria is managed by building fusional convergence (convergence exercises) or temporary base-out prism. Esophoria uses base-in/plus.
decode: Exophoria is managed by BUILDING fusional convergence (or temporary base-out prism).
ow: Plus lenses reduce convergence and suit esophoria, not exophoria.
Patching treats amblyopia, not exophoria alignment.
Base-in reduces convergence and worsens an exo demand.
Correct. Exophoria therapy increases fusional convergence.

q: Which amblyopia type generally has the worst prognosis?
w: Deprivation amblyopia (cataract, ptosis, opacity) has the worst prognosis and must be treated within the critical period.
decode: DEPRIVATION amblyopia (cataract, ptosis, opacity) has the WORST prognosis.
ow: Meridional amblyopia is milder than deprivation.
Anisometropic amblyopia has a better prognosis than deprivation.
Strabismic amblyopia is more treatable than deprivation.
Correct. Deprivation amblyopia has the worst prognosis.

q: Divergence excess shows which pattern?
o: Equal exo at near and distance
Exo greater at distance, high AC/A
Eso at distance, ortho at near
Receded NPC with exo at near
w: Divergence excess: large exo at distance, near closer to ortho, with a high AC/A.
k: DE = exo far, ortho near, high AC/A.
decode: Divergence excess shows large EXO at DISTANCE, near closer to ortho, with a high AC/A.
ow: Equal exo near and distance is basic exophoria, not divergence excess.
Correct. DE shows exo greater at distance with high AC/A.
Eso at distance is not the DE pattern.
A receded NPC with near exo describes convergence insufficiency.

q: The most common type of amblyopia is:
w: Strabismic amblyopia (suppression of a constantly deviating eye) is the most common type.
decode: STRABISMIC amblyopia (suppression of a constantly deviating eye) is the most common type.
ow: Ametropic amblyopia is less common than strabismic.
Meridional amblyopia is uncommon.
Deprivation amblyopia is rare.
Correct. Strabismic amblyopia is the most common type.

q: What is normal stereoacuity?
w: Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 seconds of arc; smaller arc-second values mean finer stereopsis.
decode: Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 seconds of arc (smaller values = finer stereo).
ow: 200–400 sec arc is coarse, not normal.
1–2 min of arc (60–120 sec) is coarser than normal.
Correct. Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 sec arc.
3000 sec arc is gross (the Titmus fly), not normal.

q: Which stereoacuity value represents the FINEST depth perception?
w: Smaller arc-second values are finer; 20 sec arc is far better than 400 sec arc.
decode: The SMALLEST arc-second value represents the FINEST stereopsis, so 20 sec arc.
ow: Correct. 20 sec arc is the finest depth perception listed.
400 sec arc is coarse.
100 sec arc is coarser than 20.
40 sec arc is normal but coarser than 20.

q: Stereopsis corresponds to which Worth grade of binocular vision?
w: Grade 3 (stereopsis) is the highest; Grade 2 is flat fusion, Grade 1 is simultaneous perception.
decode: Stereopsis corresponds to Worth GRADE 3, the highest level.
ow: Correct. Stereopsis is Worth Grade 3.
Grade 1 is simultaneous perception.
Grade 2 is flat fusion.
There is no Grade 4.

q: A patient with deep constant strabismic amblyopia (20/200) is tested on the Randot. Expected result:
w: Deep suppression and disrupted binocular neurons abolish stereopsis regardless of the dominant eye's acuity.
decode: Deep constant strabismic amblyopia abolishes stereopsis, so NO measurable stereo.
ow: Normal stereo is not expected with deep amblyopia.
Deep suppression does affect stereo, so 'unaffected' is wrong.
Correct. Deep strabismic amblyopia gives no measurable stereopsis.
It is typically absent, not merely reduced, with 20/200 deep amblyopia.

q: Which stereopsis test uses real (physical) depth and requires no special glasses?
w: The Frisby uses transparent plates of real thickness, so no polarized/red-green glasses are needed.
decode: The FRISBY uses transparent plates of real thickness, so no special glasses are needed.
ow: The Titmus needs polarized glasses.
The Randot needs polarized glasses.
The TNO needs red-green glasses.
Correct. The Frisby uses real depth and no glasses.

q: On the Titmus test, the 'fly' represents which (coarsest) disparity?
w: The Titmus fly is a gross stereo target at ~3000 sec arc, used to confirm any gross stereopsis.
decode: The Titmus FLY is the coarsest target at ~3000 sec arc.
ow: Correct. The Titmus fly is ~3000 sec arc (coarsest).
40 sec arc is a fine circles target, not the fly.
20 sec arc is finer still, not the fly.
400 sec arc is finer than the fly.

q: Stereopsis normally first develops at about:
w: Binocular cortical neurons mature so stereopsis emerges around 3–6 months; it is not present at birth.
decode: Stereopsis emerges around 3–6 months as binocular cortical neurons mature; it is not present at birth.
ow: 5 years is far too late for stereopsis onset.
2 years is later than normal onset.
Stereopsis is not present at birth.
Correct. Stereopsis develops around 3–6 months.

q: A patient who loses one eye retains depth perception from:
w: A monocular patient loses stereopsis but keeps monocular cues and adapts well for daily function.
k: Monocular cues survive loss of stereopsis.
decode: A monocular patient loses stereopsis but keeps MONOCULAR CUES for depth.
ow: Panum's fusion needs two eyes and is lost.
Retinal disparity needs two eyes and is lost.
Stereopsis is lost with one eye.
Correct. Monocular cues survive the loss of one eye.

q: Stereopsis specifically depends on:
w: Stereopsis arises from small horizontal disparities between the two retinal images within Panum's area.
decode: Stereopsis arises from small horizontal binocular RETINAL DISPARITY within Panum's area.
ow: Convergence effort alone does not create stereopsis.
Correct. Stereopsis depends on binocular retinal disparity.
Pupil-size differences do not generate stereopsis.
Accommodative demand is not the basis of stereopsis.

q: Stereopsis requires which prerequisites?
w: Stereopsis (Grade 3) is built on simultaneous perception (Grade 1) and fusion (Grade 2).
decode: Stereopsis (Grade 3) is built on simultaneous perception (Grade 1) and fusion (Grade 2) FIRST.
ow: Suppression prevents, not enables, stereopsis.
Eccentric fixation is an obstacle, not a prerequisite.
Grade 3 cannot stand without Grades 1 and 2.
Correct. Stereopsis needs Grades 1 and 2 first.

q: Convergence as a depth cue provides useful information only within about:
w: Convergence is a useful depth cue only at near (within ~2 m); beyond that, disparity and monocular cues dominate.
decode: Convergence is a useful depth cue only at near, within about 2 m.
ow: 10 m is beyond the useful convergence-cue range.
50 m is far beyond it.
Correct. Convergence is a useful depth cue only within ~2 m.
At optical infinity convergence provides no depth cue.

q: A 7-year-old with 20/20 acuity and normal BV cannot find objects on a busy worksheet and loses his place reading. Best assessment:
w: These figure-ground and sequencing problems are visual perceptual (VPS). With acuity and BV normal, TVPS-3 (pointing-only) is appropriate.
decode: Figure-ground and sequencing complaints with normal acuity/BV call for the TVPS-3.
ow: Tonometry measures IOP, unrelated to perceptual complaints.
A visual field test does not assess visual perception.
Ishihara tests color, not perceptual processing.
Correct. With 20/20 and normal BV, TVPS-3 assesses the perceptual deficit.

q: A patient has 20/20 acuity but struggles with visual processing tasks. This shows that:
o: 20/20 acuity does NOT rule out a VIP deficit
w: Visual information processing is separate from acuity; 20/20 does not exclude a VIP/VPS deficit.
k: 20/20 does not rule out VIP deficit.
decode: 20/20 acuity does NOT rule out a visual-information-processing deficit; perception is separate from acuity.
ow: Correct. 20/20 acuity does not exclude a VIP deficit.
Acuity does not equal perception.
This scenario is about processing, not eye alignment.
20/20 does not rule out a perceptual deficit.

q: How do VIP and VPS relate?
o: VPS includes motor output; VIP does not
VIP is broad; VPS is the non-motor subset
w: Visual information processing (VIP) is the broad domain; visual perceptual skills (VPS) are its non-motor subset.
decode: VIP is the broad domain; VPS are its NON-MOTOR subset.
ow: VPS is the non-motor subset; the motor split is stated backward here.
They are not identical.
Correct. VIP is broad; VPS is the non-motor subset.
VPS is not acuity.

q: The Beery VMI primarily measures:
w: Beery VMI requires copying shapes, testing visual-motor integration; a low score may be perceptual OR motor.
decode: The Beery VMI measures VISUAL-MOTOR INTEGRATION through shape copying.
ow: Correct. Beery VMI measures visual-motor integration.
It is not a non-motor perception test; copying requires motor output.
It does not measure visual fields.
It does not test color vision.

q: The TVPS-3 is best described as:
w: TVPS-3 uses pointing responses to assess all seven non-motor VPS subtopics in ages 4–18.
decode: The TVPS-3 is a NON-MOTOR VPS test (pointing responses), ages 4–18.
ow: It is not a stereo test.
Correct. TVPS-3 is a non-motor VPS test for ages 4–18.
It is not a color test.
It is deliberately motor-free, not motor-loaded.

q: A child scores poorly on the Beery VMI. To separate perception from motor output, do which test next?
w: TVPS-3 needs no motor output; if normal, the Beery deficit is motor; if poor, it is perceptual.
k: Use TVPS-3 to isolate perception from motor.
decode: TVPS-3 needs no motor output, so it separates a perceptual deficit from a motor one.
ow: Correct. TVPS-3 isolates perception from motor output.
Tonometry does not separate perception from motor.
A visual field test does not address this.
Snellen acuity does not separate perception from motor.

q: The DTVP-2 is notable because it:
w: The DTVP-2 yields both motor-reduced and motor-enhanced scores, helping localize the deficit, in ages 4–10.
decode: The DTVP-2 yields BOTH motor-reduced and motor-enhanced scores, helping localize the deficit.
ow: It does require some motor response; that is not its notable feature.
It does not measure acuity only.
Correct. DTVP-2 splits motor-free and motor scores.
It does not test color vision only.

q: Difficulty recognizing a shape when its size or orientation changes is a deficit of:
w: Form constancy is recognizing an object despite changes in size, orientation, or context.
k: Form constancy = same shape, changed size/orientation.
decode: FORM CONSTANCY is recognizing an object despite changes in size or orientation.
ow: Visual memory is recall of a form, not recognition across transformations.
Visual closure is recognizing a whole from an incomplete figure.
Figure-ground is separating an object from a busy background.
Correct. Form constancy handles changed size or orientation.

q: Identifying a complete object from an incomplete or partial drawing is the skill of:
w: Visual closure is recognizing a whole from fragmentary visual information.
k: Visual closure = whole from incomplete figure.
decode: VISUAL CLOSURE is recognizing a whole object from an incomplete or partial drawing.
ow: Figure-ground is finding an object in a busy background.
Correct. Visual closure builds the whole from a fragmentary figure.
Spatial relations concern position and orientation between objects.
Form constancy is recognizing a shape despite size or orientation changes.

q: Trouble locating a target object within a cluttered background is a deficit of:
w: Figure-ground is separating the relevant object from a busy background; failing it causes 'lost on the page' behavior.
decode: FIGURE-GROUND is separating a target object from a cluttered background.
ow: Correct. Figure-ground separates the object from a busy background.
Form constancy is recognizing a shape across size/orientation changes.
Visual closure is completing an incomplete figure.
Visual memory is recall of a form, not locating it in clutter.

q: Which assessment is most appropriate when handwriting and shape-copying are the chief complaints?
w: Copying and handwriting are visual-motor tasks, best evaluated by the Beery VMI.
decode: Handwriting and shape-copying are VISUAL-MOTOR tasks, best evaluated by the Beery VMI.
ow: TVPS-3 is motor-free and does not target copying/handwriting.
Ishihara tests color, not visual-motor integration.
Correct. Copying and handwriting complaints point to the Beery VMI.
Goldmann perimetry maps the field, unrelated to copying.

q: Cone-mediated dark adaptation is essentially complete by about:
w: Cones finish adapting at roughly 7 minutes, producing the Kohlrausch kink where cones plateau and rods take over. Full rod adaptation needs 30–40 minutes.
decode: Cone-mediated dark adaptation is essentially complete by ~7 minutes (the Kohlrausch kink).
ow: 15 minutes is past the cone plateau, into the rod branch.
Correct. Cones finish adapting at ~7 minutes.
40 minutes is full rod adaptation, not cone.
2 minutes is too early for cone completion.

q: The Kohlrausch kink on the dark adaptation curve marks:
o: The handover from cones to rods
The onset of the Purkinje shift
w: The kink at about 7 minutes is the break in the curve where cones have plateaued and the slower, more sensitive rods take over.
decode: The Kohlrausch kink marks the HANDOVER from cones to rods (~7 min).
ow: Peak rod sensitivity comes later, at full adaptation, not at the kink.
Correct. The kink is the cone-to-rod handover.
Complete dark adaptation is at 30–40 min, not the kink.
The Purkinje shift is a spectral change, not the curve inflection.

q: The Purkinje shift describes the peak sensitivity moving:
w: Going from photopic to scotopic conditions, peak sensitivity shifts from 555 nm (cones, yellow-green) to 507 nm (rods, blue-green). This is why reds look black at dusk while blues stay visible.
decode: The Purkinje shift moves peak sensitivity FROM 555 nm TO 507 nm as light fades.
ow: Correct. Purkinje shift: 555 nm (cones) to 507 nm (rods).
555 to 750 nm is not the Purkinje direction.
440 to 507 nm is not the Purkinje shift.
507 to 555 nm is the reverse (going brighter).

q: Retinal pH in the dark compared with the light is:
w: The dark retina sits at about pH 7.3 (alkaline); in light it falls to roughly 7.0 (acidic).
decode: The dark retina is more ALKALINE (~pH 7.3); in light it falls toward 7.0.
ow: It is not fixed at a neutral 7.0 in the dark.
Retinal pH does change with light state.
Correct. The dark retina is more alkaline (~7.3).
The dark retina is alkaline, not more acidic.

q: Angle alpha is the angle between the optical and visual axes measured at the:
w: Angle alpha is subtended at the nodal point and averages about 5° temporal. A large positive angle kappa mimics exotropia.
k: Angle alpha = at the nodal point, ~5° temporal.
decode: Angle alpha (optical vs visual axis) is subtended at the NODAL point, ~5° temporal.
ow: The entrance pupil is the reference for angle kappa, not alpha.
The corneal apex is not the alpha reference.
Correct. Angle alpha is measured at the nodal point.
The center of rotation is where Fick axes cross, not the alpha reference.

q: A positive angle kappa produces the appearance of:
w: With a positive kappa the corneal reflex sits nasally, making the eye look turned out. It is an artifact of reflex position, not a real deviation.
decode: A POSITIVE angle kappa (reflex nasal) produces the appearance of PSEUDO-EXOTROPIA.
ow: Pseudo-esotropia comes from a negative kappa.
Positive kappa does not mimic hypertropia.
Correct. Positive kappa gives pseudo-exotropia.
It is an artifact of reflex position, not a true exotropia.

q: Ricco's law of spatial summation states that:
w: Ricco's law covers spatial summation: within the summation area, threshold depends on the product of area and intensity. Bunsen-Roscoe is the temporal analogue, where time × intensity is constant.
k: Ricco = area × intensity; Bunsen-Roscoe = time × intensity.
decode: Ricco's law of spatial summation: within the summation area, AREA × INTENSITY is constant.
ow: Intensity ÷ time is not Ricco's form.
Area ÷ intensity is not the correct relationship.
Time × intensity is the temporal (Bunsen-Roscoe) law.
Correct. Ricco's law: area × intensity is constant.

q: The red-sensitive cone pigment is called:
w: Erythrolabe is the long-wavelength (red) pigment, chlorolabe the middle (green), and cyanolabe the short (blue).
k: Erythrolabe R, chlorolabe G, cyanolabe B.
decode: ERYTHROLABE is the long-wavelength (red) cone pigment.
ow: Chlorolabe is the green (middle) pigment.
Rhodopsin is the rod pigment.
Cyanolabe is the blue (short) pigment.
Correct. Erythrolabe is the red cone pigment.

q: The longest axis of the globe, the anteroposterior axis, measures about:
w: The AP (Y) axis is about 24 mm and is the longest; the vertical and horizontal axes run about 22 mm each.
decode: The anteroposterior (Y) axis is the longest, about 24 mm.
ow: 20 mm is too short for the AP axis.
22 mm is the vertical/horizontal axis length.
Correct. The AP axis is ~24 mm, the longest.
26 mm overstates the AP axis.

q: Which LGB layers receive crossed (nasal) fibers?
w: Layers 1, 4 and 6 take contralateral crossed nasal fibers; layers 2, 3 and 5 take ipsilateral uncrossed temporal fibers.
decode: LGB layers 1, 4, 6 receive CROSSED (nasal, contralateral) fibers.
ow: Layers 1, 2, 3 mix sides incorrectly here.
Correct. Layers 1, 4, 6 take crossed nasal fibers.
Layers 2, 3, 5 take uncrossed temporal fibers.
Layers 4, 5, 6 mix sides incorrectly.

q: Brodmann area 18 is known as the:
w: Area 17 is striate (primary), 18 is parastriate (secondary), and 19 is peristriate (higher-order).
decode: Brodmann area 18 is the PARASTRIATE cortex.
ow: Peristriate cortex is area 19, not 18.
Striate cortex is area 17.
Correct. Area 18 is the parastriate cortex.
There is no 'prestriate motor area' by this label; 18 is parastriate.

q: Which visual function fails earliest in optic nerve disease?
w: Color is the most vulnerable function and drops out first, which is why red desaturation is an early optic neuritis sign. Motion is the most resilient and goes last.
k: Color fails first; motion survives longest.
decode: COLOR VISION fails earliest in optic nerve disease (basis of red desaturation).
ow: Visual acuity is more resilient than color early on.
Light projection is a very late, gross function.
Correct. Color vision fails earliest.
Motion perception is the most resilient, lost last.

q: The dorsal stream to the parietal lobe processes:
w: The dorsal 'where/how' stream handles spatial relationships and motion; the ventral 'what' stream in the temporal lobe handles object recognition.
decode: The DORSAL stream to the parietal lobe processes SPATIAL LOCATION and MOTION.
ow: Color constancy is a ventral-stream function.
Face recognition is ventral-stream.
Object identity is the ventral 'what' stream.
Correct. The dorsal stream handles spatial location and motion.

q: The normal temporal extent of the monocular visual field is about:
w: Normal extents run superior 60°, inferior 75°, temporal 100°, nasal 60°. The temporal field is widest because the nose blocks nothing on that side.
decode: The TEMPORAL field is widest at 100° (S60, I75, N60).
ow: 60° is the nasal/superior extent.
75° is the inferior extent.
90° is not the temporal maximum.
Correct. The temporal extent is 100°.

q: The monocular temporal crescent measures roughly:
w: The temporal crescent is the outer 30° seen by one eye alone, beyond the 120° of binocular overlap.
decode: The monocular temporal crescent is the outer ~30°, beyond the 120° binocular overlap.
ow: 10° understates the crescent.
Correct. The temporal crescent is ~30° each side.
60° is too wide for the crescent.
100° is the whole temporal extent, not the crescent.

q: Which Goldmann stimulus size is used to map the far periphery in advanced field loss?
w: Size V is the largest stimulus at 64 mm². The V4e isopter maps residual peripheral field in retinitis pigmentosa and low vision. Size I is smallest at 0.25 mm².
k: V = largest (64 mm²); I = smallest (0.25 mm²).
decode: Goldmann size V (64 mm²) maps the far periphery in advanced field loss.
ow: Size I (0.25 mm²) is the smallest, used for fine central testing.
Correct. Size V is the largest, used for far-peripheral mapping.
Size III is the standard mid-range, not the largest.
Size II is smaller than V.

q: On the Amsler grid, one small square subtends:
w: Each square equals 1° of visual field, and the whole grid covers the central 10° at the standard 30 cm working distance.
decode: Each Amsler square subtends 1°, and the grid covers the central 10°.
ow: 1 arc minute is far too small for one square.
Correct. One Amsler square subtends 1°.
5° is too large for a single square.
5 arc minutes is far too small.

q: A 'pie in the sky' superior quadrantanopia localizes to:
w: Meyer's loop carries inferior retinal fibers through the temporal lobe, so a lesion there drops the contralateral superior quadrant: pie in the sky.
k: Pie in the sky = Meyer's loop, temporal lobe.
decode: A 'pie in the sky' superior quadrantanopia localizes to MEYER'S LOOP in the temporal lobe.
ow: Correct. Meyer's loop carries inferior fibers through the temporal lobe.
The occipital pole lesion gives a congruous macular-splitting defect, not a temporal-lobe quadrantanopia.
The chiasm gives bitemporal hemianopia.
Parietal radiation lesions give an inferior ('pie on the floor') defect.

q: The trichromatic theory of Young-Helmholtz explains color coding at the level of the:
w: Young-Helmholtz trichromacy operates at the receptor level with three cone types. Hering's opponent process explains post-receptor coding, and stage theory reconciles the two.
decode: Young-Helmholtz trichromacy operates at the PHOTORECEPTOR level (three cone types).
ow: The lateral geniculate is post-receptor, not the trichromatic site.
The striate cortex is post-receptor.
Correct. Trichromacy operates at the photoreceptors.
Ganglion cells are post-receptor (opponent) processing.

q: The opponent process theory of color vision was proposed by:
w: Hering's opponent process describes red-green, blue-yellow and black-white channels beyond the receptors, explaining afterimages and why no color looks reddish-green.
decode: HERING proposed the OPPONENT-PROCESS theory (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white).
ow: Ladd-Franklin proposed an evolutionary theory.
Correct. Hering proposed the opponent-process theory.
Young and Helmholtz proposed trichromacy.
Purkinje is known for the dim-light sensitivity shift.

q: The most common inherited color vision defect is:
w: Deuteranomaly, a green weakness rather than a total loss, is the commonest defect. Red-green deficiency overall affects about 8% of males.
decode: DEUTERANOMALY (green weakness) is the most common inherited color defect.
ow: Correct. Deuteranomaly is the commonest defect.
Protanopia is less common than deuteranomaly.
Tritanomaly is rare.
Deuteranopia (total green loss) is less common than deuteranomaly.

q: The first plate of the Ishihara test shows '12' because it is:
o: A control plate everyone can read
w: Plate 1 is a demonstration plate visible to all observers, including total color defectives. Failing it suggests malingering or very poor acuity rather than a color defect.
decode: Ishihara plate 1 ('12') is a CONTROL plate everyone, including color-defectives, can read.
ow: It is not a tritan plate.
Correct. Plate 1 is the control everyone reads.
It is the easiest, demonstration plate, not the hardest.
It is not a red-green screening plate; it screens nothing.

q: The most comprehensive clinical test of color discrimination is the:
w: The Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue arranges caps by subtle hue steps and grades severity as well as type. Ishihara only screens red-green.
decode: The FM-100 Hue test is the most comprehensive, grading axis and severity of a color defect.
ow: Ishihara only screens red-green.
HRR screens red-green and blue-yellow but does not grade severity as finely.
The D-15 sorts a short cap set; it is a screener, less detailed than FM-100.
Correct. FM-100 Hue is the most comprehensive test.

q: The FALANT occupational color test is performed at:
w: The Farnsworth Lantern is run at 8 feet and simulates signal-light recognition for maritime and aviation screening.
decode: The FALANT occupational lantern test is performed at 8 feet.
ow: 20 feet is not the FALANT working distance.
40 cm is a near distance, not the FALANT setup.
1 meter is not the standard FALANT distance.
Correct. FALANT is performed at 8 feet.

q: The normal AC/A ratio is about:
w: Normal AC/A runs 4:1 to 6:1. It is high in convergence excess and divergence excess, and low in convergence and divergence insufficiency.
decode: Normal AC/A is 4:1 to 6:1.
ow: 1:1 to 2:1 is abnormally low.
8:1 to 10:1 is high.
12:1 is very high.
Correct. Normal AC/A is 4:1 to 6:1.

q: The slowest of the eye movements is:
w: Vergence is slowest at about 20°/s. The VOR is fastest with a 15 ms latency; saccades have a 200 ms latency.
decode: VERGENCE is the slowest eye movement (~20°/s); the VOR is fastest.
ow: Smooth pursuit is faster than vergence.
The saccade is fast, not the slowest.
Correct. Vergence is the slowest movement.
The VOR is the fastest reflex, not the slowest.

q: Sheard's criterion requires the fusional reserve to be at least:
w: Sheard's criterion holds that the opposing fusional reserve should be at least twice the phoria for comfortable single vision. Failing it supports prescribing prism or starting therapy.
decode: Sheard's criterion requires the fusional reserve to be at least TWICE the phoria.
ow: Half the phoria is far below Sheard's requirement.
Equal to the phoria is below the threshold.
Correct. Sheard's requires reserve ≥ 2× the phoria.
Three times the phoria overstates the rule.

q: Worth Grade 1 of binocular vision is:
w: Grade 1 is simultaneous perception, Grade 2 flat fusion with amplitude, Grade 3 stereopsis. Grades 1 and 2 are prerequisites for Grade 3.
decode: Worth Grade 1 is SIMULTANEOUS macular perception.
ow: Flat fusion with amplitude is Grade 2.
Stereopsis is Grade 3.
Correct. Grade 1 is simultaneous perception.
Suppression is not a Worth fusion grade.

q: Physiologic diplopia for an object beyond the fixation point is:
w: Objects farther than fixation give uncrossed physiologic diplopia; objects nearer than fixation give crossed diplopia. It is a normal finding and a useful anti-suppression cue.
decode: An object BEYOND fixation gives UNCROSSED physiologic diplopia.
ow: Crossed diplopia is for objects nearer than fixation.
Correct. Far objects give uncrossed diplopia.
Physiologic diplopia is present, not absent, off the fixation point.
It is horizontal, not vertical.

q: The normal near point of convergence is:
w: A normal NPC breaks at 8 cm or closer. Beyond 10 cm suggests convergence insufficiency.
decode: Normal NPC breaks at ≤8 cm; beyond ~10 cm suggests convergence insufficiency.
ow: ≤15 cm is receded, not normal.
≤2 cm is closer than the typical normal break.
Correct. Normal NPC break is ≤8 cm.
≤20 cm is markedly receded.

q: Normal stereoacuity is about:
w: Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 arc seconds. The Randot resolves to about 20 arc seconds; the Titmus fly is the coarsest target at 3000 arc seconds.
decode: Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 arc seconds.
ow: Correct. Normal stereoacuity is 20–40 arc sec.
100–200 arc sec is coarse.
1–2 min of arc (60–120 sec) is coarser than normal.
5–10 arc sec is finer than typical normal.

q: Panum's fusional area at the fovea spans about:
w: Panum's area is the zone of disparity within which two retinal images still fuse into one. It is narrowest at the fovea (6–10 arc min) and widens peripherally.
decode: Panum's fusional area at the fovea spans about 6–10 arc minutes and widens peripherally.
ow: Correct. Panum's area at the fovea is 6–10 arc min.
30–60 arc min is a peripheral, not foveal, width.
1–2 arc min understates the foveal area.
2–3 degrees is far too wide for the fovea.

q: The coarsest target on the Titmus stereotest is the:
w: The Titmus fly is 3000 arc seconds, gross enough that a patient with no stereopsis may still pass it by monocular cues, so it is a screen rather than a measure.
decode: The Titmus FLY is the coarsest target (~3000 arc sec).
ow: Correct. The Titmus fly is the coarsest target.
The animals are finer than the fly.
The circles are the fine graded target.
Randot forms are not part of the Titmus fly.

q: The relationship between VIP and VPS is that:
o: VPS is the non-motor subset of VIP
VIP is a subset of VPS
w: Visual information processing is the broad term covering processing plus motor output. Visual perceptual skills are the non-motor subset within it.
k: VIP broad; VPS = its non-motor subset.
decode: VPS are the NON-MOTOR subset within the broader VIP domain.
ow: Correct. VPS is the non-motor subset of VIP.
VIP is the broader term, not a subset of VPS.
They are not interchangeable.
VIP as a whole includes motor output, so 'neither involves motor' is wrong.

q: The Beery VMI assesses a child primarily by asking them to:
w: The Beery VMI measures visual-motor integration through shape copying and spans ages 2 to 100. The TVPS-3 is deliberately non-motor and uses pointing only.
decode: The Beery VMI asks the child to COPY geometric shapes (visual-motor integration).
ow: Correct. The Beery VMI uses shape copying.
Sorting by color is not the Beery task.
Pointing to a match is the TVPS-3 method.
Naming shapes aloud is not the Beery task.

q: The TVPS-3 is designed to be motor-free by having the child:
w: The TVPS-3 requires pointing only, so a child with poor motor skills is not penalized on a perceptual test. It covers ages 4 to 18.
decode: The TVPS-3 is motor-free: the child POINTS to the answer.
ow: Tracing adds motor demand, unlike the TVPS-3.
Correct. TVPS-3 uses pointing only.
Drawing the target adds motor demand.
Assembling blocks is a motor task, not TVPS-3.

q: Horizontal eye movements (adduction and abduction) occur around which axis?
w: The Z (vertical) axis governs horizontal movement, the X axis governs vertical movement, and the Y (anteroposterior) axis governs torsion. The axis is named for the line the eye rotates around, not the direction it moves.
k: Z = horizontal, X = vertical, Y = torsion.
decode: Horizontal movements occur about the Z (vertical) axis; the axis is named for the line the eye rotates around.
ow: The visual axis is a line of sight, not a rotation axis for horizontal movement.
The Y (AP) axis governs torsion.
Correct. The Z (vertical) axis governs horizontal movement.
The X axis governs vertical movement.

q: Angle kappa, unlike angle alpha, is measured at the:
w: Angle kappa is subtended at the pupil; angle alpha at the nodal point. Both describe the offset between the optical and visual axes, but at different reference points.
k: Kappa at the pupil; alpha at the nodal point.
decode: Angle KAPPA is measured at the PUPIL; alpha at the nodal point.
ow: Correct. Angle kappa is measured at the pupil.
The nodal point is the reference for angle alpha.
The center of rotation is where Fick axes cross.
The fovea is where the visual axis lands, not the kappa reference.

q: A positive angle kappa on Hirschberg testing is distinguished from true exotropia by:
w: Positive kappa shifts the reflex temporally, mimicking exotropia, but the cover test shows no movement because there is no true deviation. It is pseudo-exotropia.
k: Pseudo-exotropia: reflex shifted, cover test negative.
decode: Positive kappa mimics exotropia but shows a NEGATIVE cover test (no true deviation).
ow: Reflex displacement size does not distinguish it; the cover test does.
Correct. A negative cover test distinguishes pseudo- from true exotropia.
Diplopia is not the distinguishing feature here.
A red filter is not needed to make this distinction.

q: The 30° monocular crescent at each side of the field is seen by the:
w: The central 120° is binocular. Beyond it, each temporal retina alone sees a 30° crescent, which is why a chiasmal lesion costs those far temporal fields.
k: Monocular crescent = 30°, seen by temporal retina.
decode: The 30° monocular crescent is seen by the TEMPORAL retina alone.
ow: The superior retina does not define the temporal crescent.
The nasal retina sees the temporal field but the crescent input is from temporal retina of that eye.
Correct. The temporal retina alone sees the 30° crescent.
The fovea sees central, not peripheral crescent, field.

q: In protanopia, red objects appear:
w: Protanopes lack L-cones, and red light stimulates the M- and S-cones poorly, so red loses luminance as well as hue. A red traffic light can look almost black.
decode: Protanopes lack L-cones, so red loses luminance and appears ABNORMALLY DIM.
ow: Red does not appear brighter to a protanope.
Red brightness is not unchanged; it is reduced.
Correct. Red appears abnormally dim in protanopia.
Red does not turn bright blue.

q: Tritanopia differs from the red-green defects in that it is:
w: Tritan defects are autosomal and rare, so they affect the sexes equally. Red-green defects are X-linked, which is why they hit about 8% of males.
decode: Tritan defects are AUTOSOMAL and RARE, affecting the sexes equally.
ow: Tritan defects are rare, not the most common.
They are not confined to females.
They are autosomal, not X-linked recessive like red-green.
Correct. Tritanopia is autosomal and rare.

q: On the FM-100 Hue test, the patient responds by:
w: The FM-100 uses hue-graded caps the patient arranges in sequence, and the error score grades severity and type. Ishihara uses numerals and HRR uses symbols.
decode: On the FM-100 Hue test the patient ARRANGES caps in hue order.
ow: Naming the color is not the FM-100 task.
Tracing a path is not the FM-100 method.
Reading a number is the Ishihara task.
Correct. FM-100 requires arranging caps in hue order.

q: The fastest VOLUNTARY eye movement is the:
w: The saccade is the fastest voluntary movement, at a 200 ms latency. The VOR is the fastest reflex at 15 ms but is not voluntary, and vergence is slowest at 20°/s.
k: Saccade fastest voluntary; VOR fastest reflex.
decode: The SACCADE is the fastest VOLUNTARY eye movement.
ow: Smooth pursuit is slower than a saccade.
Correct. The saccade is the fastest voluntary movement.
Vergence is the slowest movement.
The VOR is faster but is a reflex, not voluntary.

q: Convergence insufficiency is characterized by an AC/A ratio that is:
w: CI carries a low AC/A: accommodating produces too little convergence. High AC/A drives the excess conditions, convergence excess and divergence excess.
k: CI = low AC/A; excess conditions = high AC/A.
decode: Convergence insufficiency carries a LOW AC/A (too little convergence per diopter).
ow: Correct. CI has a low AC/A.
High AC/A drives the excess conditions, not CI.
The AC/A in CI is characteristically low, not simply variable.
A normal AC/A does not define CI.

q: Why does a heterophoria preserve normal retinal correspondence?
o: The angle is too small to adapt
w: A phoria is compensated by fusion nearly all the time, so the eyes stay aligned and NRC persists. ARC needs the constant, unchanging misalignment of a constant strabismus.
k: Phoria keeps NRC; constant strabismus breeds ARC.
decode: A heterophoria keeps the EYES ALIGNED by fusion most of the time, preserving normal correspondence.
ow: Correct. Because the eyes stay aligned, NRC persists.
Phorias are not always intermittent; the point is fusion keeps alignment.
Fusion is present in a phoria, not permanently absent.
A phoria's angle is not too small to adapt; the reason is maintained alignment.

q: Suppression treated early within the critical period is:
w: Suppression itself is reversible when treated early. The danger is that prolonged suppression breeds amblyopia, which becomes permanent once the critical period closes around 7 to 8 years.
k: Suppression reversible early; untreated it becomes amblyopia.
decode: Suppression treated early within the critical period is REVERSIBLE.
ow: Correct. Early treatment makes suppression reversible.
It is not permanent regardless of therapy when treated early.
It is treatable during the critical period, not untreatable after age 3.
It does not require surgery to correct.

q: During Hirschberg testing, the corneal light reflex falls approximately 1mm temporal to the corneal center in both eyes. Cover test reveals no movement. What is the most likely explanation?
w: Positive angle kappa exists when the center of the entrance pupil is nasal to the visual axis. Because the pupil is nasal, the corneal light reflex appears displaced temporally — simulating exotropia on Hirschberg. The negative cover test confirms no real deviation is present. This is pseudo-exotropia due to positive angle kappa. Negative kappa would produce a nasal reflex displacement (pseudo-esotropia). Angle alpha is measured at the nodal point and does not produce this clinical finding directly.
k: Positive angle kappa exists when the center of the entrance pupil is nasal to the visual axis.
decode: A reflex ~1 mm TEMPORAL in both eyes with a negative cover test is POSITIVE angle kappa (pseudo-exotropia).
ow: Bilateral exotropia would move on cover test; here there is none.
Angle alpha is measured at the nodal point and does not produce this reflex-plus-negative-cover picture.
Correct. Positive kappa puts the pupil nasal, so the reflex looks temporal with no true deviation.
Negative kappa gives a nasal reflex (pseudo-esotropia), the opposite.

q: A patient is tested in a dark room after 40 minutes of adaptation. At what wavelength of monochromatic light would their visual threshold be lowest?
w: After 40 minutes of dark adaptation, the visual system is operating in scotopic mode — driven entirely by rods. Rods have maximum sensitivity at approximately 507 nm (blue-green). The 555 nm peak applies to photopic (cone-driven) conditions. 440 nm is the S-cone peak (cyanolabe), relevant in photopic color vision. 535 nm is the M-cone (chlorolabe) peak. In scotopic conditions, all three cone types are essentially inactive, and rod sensitivity dominates.
k: After 40 minutes of dark adaptation, the visual system is operating in scotopic mode — driven entirely by…
decode: After 40 min of dark adaptation vision is SCOTOPIC (rod-driven); threshold is lowest near 507 nm.
ow: 440 nm is the S-cone (photopic) peak.
Correct. Rod-driven scotopic vision peaks near 507 nm.
535 nm is the M-cone (green) peak.
555 nm is the photopic cone peak, not scotopic.

q: A patient's rhodopsin cannot regenerate after light exposure. Which step in the visual cycle is most likely impaired?
o: Re-isomerization of all-trans retinal to 11-cis retinal in the RPE
Release of glutamate at the synaptic terminal in the dark
Transport of all-trans retinal from photoreceptors to RPE
Photoisomerization of 11-cis retinal in the outer segment
w: Rhodopsin regeneration depends on recycling spent chromophore (all-trans retinal) back to its usable form (11-cis retinal). This enzymatic re-isomerization occurs in the RPE, not in the photoreceptor outer segment. After light hits rhodopsin, 11-cis retinal photoisomerizes to all-trans (this is the TRIGGER, not the regeneration step). All-trans retinal exits the photoreceptor and enters the RPE where the RPE65 enzyme converts it back to 11-cis retinal. RPE65 mutations cause Leber congenital amaurosis — a genetic cause of severe visual impairment. Transport is a prerequisite for C but not the regeneration step itself. Glutamate release is the dark-current synapse activity, unrelated to regeneration.
k: Rhodopsin regeneration depends on recycling spent chromophore (all-trans retinal) back to its usable form…
decode: Rhodopsin regeneration is the RPE RE-ISOMERIZATION of all-trans back to 11-cis retinal; block it and rhodopsin cannot regenerate.
ow: Correct. Re-isomerization in the RPE is the regeneration step.
Dark-current glutamate release is unrelated to regeneration.
Transport is a prerequisite but not the regeneration step itself.
Photoisomerization is the light trigger, not the regeneration.

q: A patient with multiple sclerosis has early optic neuritis. Which of the following visual functions would be affected earliest?
w: Color is the most vulnerable visual function — it is selectively affected early in optic nerve disease because color perception depends on intact, well-myelinated, high-frequency nerve fiber conduction. Even subtle demyelination (as in early optic neuritis) preferentially disrupts color transmission before form or motion are noticeably impaired. This is the basis of the "red desaturation" test — patients with early optic neuritis report that a bright red target appears washed-out or pink in the affected eye compared to the normal eye. Motion is the most resilient function and is typically preserved until late disease.
k: Color is the most vulnerable visual function — it is selectively affected early in optic nerve disease…
decode: COLOR perception is the most vulnerable function and fails earliest in optic neuritis.
ow: Correct. Color is selectively affected earliest in optic nerve disease.
Form perception is more resilient than color.
Motion is the most resilient function, lost last.
Contrast sensitivity is affected later than color.
